105.bp: A 3D model for film, games, or interactive work is often stored as a triangle surface: many corner points in space, plus instructions saying which corners join into triangular faces. The hard part is not only placing the points. The shape also needs the right connections, because those connections decide whether a toy has a clean shell, whether a character part is open or closed, and whether later tools can render, edit, or animate it. The abstract says common generation systems turn this surface into a sequence and predict it piece by piece. That is a poor match for a whole object, because the object is meant to be understood at once: the left side, right side, holes, handles, and thin parts all constrain one another. Nexus aims to generate the point locations and the connection pattern as two related but separate problems, so the shape can be built more globally.
105.wh: The central difficulty is that a triangle surface has two kinds of information that behave differently. Point locations are spatial: they say where corners sit in three-dimensional space. Connectivity is relational: it says which points become edges and faces. A simple list mixes these together, so the generator must decide the next list item while remembering every earlier choice. If an early point or face is wrong, later predictions inherit that mistake. The abstract calls this error accumulation. It also says the usual sequential process struggles during inference, meaning the act of producing a finished shape is not efficient. Complex objects make the tension worse, because a surface can have branches, holes, thin sheets, and disconnected-looking local pieces that still need a consistent global connection pattern. The method needs to avoid treating a whole shape as a fragile sentence where one bad word can damage everything after it.
105.naive: A smart first attempt would be to write the entire triangle surface as a long recipe: point one is here, point two is there, these three points form a face, then continue until the object is done. A model could learn to write that recipe from examples. This fails for the same reason long construction instructions are brittle. The order is artificial, but the shape is not. A chair leg does not naturally come before a chair seat in a single correct sequence. If the generator makes one bad connection early, the remaining recipe must work around a broken partial object. The abstract also suggests that earlier two-stage baselines do not solve the full problem well, because separating steps without a strong global recovery of connections can still lose the intended surface structure.
105.ap: Nexus splits the job according to what each part of the surface means. First it generates the vertices, the corner points of the triangles. It treats those points as sparse occupied cells in a three-dimensional grid that is organized as an octree, a coarse-to-fine box hierarchy where big boxes are refined only where detail is needed. A diffusion model, meaning a learned process that starts from disorder and repeatedly cleans it into a structured result, creates these vertices from rough layout to finer placement. Second, Nexus generates the connection information. It uses Space-time Interval, described as an extension of Spacetime Distance, to turn arbitrary edge and face relationships into continuous per-vertex codes. Instead of directly writing every triangle in order, another diffusion process generates these codes on the produced vertices, and the final triangle connections are recovered globally from them.
105.mech: The input evidence described in the abstract is a learned setting built from 3D shape data, including Objaverse and Toys4K, plus tests on in-the-wild images. The mechanism begins by representing candidate corner points as sparse cells in a nested 3D grid. At the coarsest level, the system only needs to decide the broad occupation pattern: where the object roughly exists. The octree then lets it refine only occupied regions, so detail is added where the shape needs it instead of across empty space. A diffusion generator performs this coarse-to-fine cleanup, producing vertex positions for the final triangle surface. Once the points exist, the method does not ask for triangles one after another. It assigns each vertex a continuous code that is meant to contain enough relational information to recover edges and faces. Space-time Interval is the paper's named way of encoding those relationships, and the abstract says it can cover arbitrary edge and face connection patterns. A second diffusion generator creates these per-vertex codes on top of the generated vertices. The system then decodes the codes globally, so the final output is a triangle surface with both point locations and a recovered connection pattern.
105.math: The main mathematical split is between positions and relations. Positions live in ordinary three-dimensional space: each vertex is a point with coordinates. Relations form a connection pattern: this point is joined to that point, and groups of points make triangular faces. Nexus uses a sparse voxel octree for the first part. A voxel is a small 3D box, and an octree is a nested set of boxes that can be split into eight smaller boxes when more detail is needed. This fits the problem because most of space is empty, while the surface occupies only a thin part of it. The generator can spend resolution on occupied regions. Diffusion supplies another idea: start with a noisy or unformed state and repeatedly move it toward examples of valid shapes. For the connection part, the abstract's Space-time Interval changes a discrete graph-like problem into continuous per-vertex embeddings, meaning each point carries numbers that summarize how it should connect. The tradeoff is directness versus global consistency. A direct triangle list is exact but brittle; continuous codes are indirect, but they give the model a smoother space in which nearby choices can be adjusted together before recovering faces.
105.dots: This paper sits beside several recurring SIGGRAPH problems. It connects to shape reconstruction because both tasks must turn incomplete or learned evidence into a usable triangle surface. It also connects to generative 3D work, where the challenge is to create objects that are not merely clouds of points but editable surfaces with meaningful connections. The abstract's separation of vertices from connection pattern echoes a wider graphics habit: split a hard object into measurements that are easier to model, then solve the relationships afterward. It also neighbors extraction papers such as the DCx paper in this same batch, because both care about how a surface's connection pattern is recovered without breaking difficult cases. The difference is that Nexus generates the shape, while DCx extracts a surface from a distance representation. Both show that the deeper issue is not just where the surface is, but how nearby pieces are allowed to join.
105.ww: The approach should improve on sequential generation because it removes an artificial ordering from a naturally spatial object. Vertices can be generated as a whole distribution over space, so far-apart parts of the object can be coordinated during the same cleaning process. The octree helps because coarse structure is decided before fine detail, which matches how shapes are organized: a toy's overall body matters before tiny protrusions. The connection step works for a different reason. Edge and face choices are highly dependent on one another, so predicting them locally or in a list can create contradictions. Per-vertex continuous codes give the system a way to store relational intent at each point, then recover the final connectivity with a global view. The abstract claims this circumvents limitations of sequential surface modeling, which is plausible because fewer choices are locked in before the system has seen the whole object.
105.po: The payoff is a native generator for triangle surfaces, not just an image-like or point-only shape. The abstract reports stronger results than autoregressive and two-stage baselines on Objaverse and Toys4K, plus demonstrations from in-the-wild images. It also reports a blind user study in which 3D practitioners preferred the outputs. Grounded in those claims, the capability is practical shape generation for film, games, and interactive 3D workflows where downstream tools expect connected triangles, not only scattered surface samples that must later be repaired.
105.limits: The abstract supports claims about the tested datasets, image demonstrations, and the user study, but it does not prove universal success on every object category or production asset. The method assumes that vertices can be well represented as sparse octree cells and that the continuous per-vertex codes contain enough information to recover the intended edges and faces. It also depends on learned examples, so behavior outside the training distribution is not established by the abstract. Complex connectivity is claimed, but the exact failure cases and editing behavior are not visible here.

106.bp: When a large physical object vibrates, every part can move in a pattern that depends on the whole object. Engineers and graphics researchers often want these natural motion patterns because they let a system predict shaking, sound-like motion, or deformation without simulating every tiny movement directly. The full calculation can become enormous, so Component Mode Synthesis divides the object into substructures, solves smaller vibration problems, and combines their motion patterns into an approximate answer for the whole domain. This paper starts from a weakness in that shortcut. A single way of cutting the domain into parts gives each substructure a limited view of how the full object can move. The proposed method builds a richer set of motion building blocks by using several spatially staggered partitions, meaning the cuts are shifted so different local pieces reveal different vibration information.
106.wh: The hard part is that a vibration pattern is both local and global. Local material pieces have their own ways of moving, but the final mode of the full domain must also agree across boundaries where pieces touch. Standard Component Mode Synthesis saves work by using substructure modes as basis functions, which are reusable building blocks for motion. The abstract says these bases do not span the desired solution space efficiently. In plain terms, the chosen building blocks do not point in the directions where the correct answer lives, so adding more of them improves the result slowly. Large-scale computation adds another pressure: the method must work across distributed computing ranks, where too much communication between machines can erase the benefit of splitting the problem. The challenge is to make the smaller solves expressive enough without making interfaces and communication too expensive.
106.naive: A beginner would split the object into chunks once, compute many natural vibration patterns for each chunk, and stitch them together. If the answer is inaccurate, the beginner would keep adding more local patterns. The abstract explains why that is wasteful: the errors decrease slowly because the single partition's building blocks do not efficiently cover the full solution space. Another naive choice is to keep a detailed basis on every interface, because the boundaries seem important. That can make the interface representation costly in time, memory, and communication. The method needs better directions for the answer, not just more directions from the same cut.
106.ap: The central move is to ask the same object for local vibration information through several different cuts. Each partition divides the domain into substructures, but the partitions are spatially staggered, so their boundaries fall in different places. A motion pattern that is awkward under one cut may be natural under another. By combining substructure eigenmodes from multiple partitions, the method forms a subspace, a smaller mathematical room in which the answer is searched, that better covers the true whole-object vibration behavior. To reduce cost further, the method does not keep expensive detailed bases on substructure interfaces. It replaces them with low-frequency approximations excited by eigenmodes from other partitions. Low-frequency here means broad, slowly varying boundary behavior, the part most likely to matter for large-scale vibration. The result keeps the Component Mode Synthesis benefits while making its building blocks more effective.
106.mech: The input is a large domain whose vibration modes are needed, plus several ways of partitioning that domain into substructures. For each partition, the method solves smaller eigenvalue problems on the substructures. An eigenvalue problem asks for motion patterns that reproduce themselves under the system's physical stiffness and mass relationships, with a number attached that describes the vibration frequency. Instead of trusting one partition's substructure modes, the method collects modes from multiple staggered partitions. These modes become candidate building blocks for the reduced global solve. The global problem is then solved in this combined subspace, so it searches among motions suggested by many different local cuts. At the interfaces, where substructures meet and must agree, the method uses cheaper low-frequency approximations rather than full detailed interface bases. The abstract says those approximations are excited from substructure eigenmodes of other partitions, so information from one cut helps represent boundary behavior in another. The output is an approximate set of global vibration modes and frequencies. The reported result is much lower error, better time and memory scaling, fast local updates, and low communication between MPI ranks on distributed clusters.
106.math: The mathematical object at the center is a vibration mode. Imagine pushing a structure and watching it settle into a pattern where all points move together at one frequency; that pattern is an eigenmode. The eigenvalue problem finds these special patterns by balancing mass and stiffness. Component Mode Synthesis reduces the full problem by choosing a basis, a set of allowed motion shapes, and solving only inside the smaller space made by combining them. The danger is that a poor basis can miss the true motion, like trying to describe a diagonal line using only horizontal strokes. Multiple partitions improve the basis because each cut exposes different local motions and different boundary constraints. The interface approximation uses a frequency tradeoff. High-frequency boundary wiggles are detailed and costly; low-frequency interface motion captures broad agreement between parts with fewer numbers. The mathematical principle is projection: instead of solving in the impossible full space, solve in a carefully chosen smaller space. The paper's claim is that staggered partitions make that smaller space point much closer to the true answer while preserving the same physical equations.
106.dots: This paper connects to physical simulation because it tries to preserve the behavior of a large object while avoiding a full costly solve. It also connects to the broader SIGGRAPH idea of reduced models: keep the motions or shapes that matter most, discard detail that has little effect on the output, and make the reduced version fast enough for large scenes or repeated updates. It neighbors geometry-processing work because the way the domain is partitioned changes the quality of the answer, much like changing coordinates can make a shape problem easier. It also relates to systems papers through MPI scaling: the mathematics is only useful if it respects memory limits and communication costs. Compared with generative papers in the batch, this one is not learning from examples; it is improving the mathematical search space for a physics-derived problem.
106.ww: The method works because a single partition accidentally hides some whole-object motions. A boundary might cut through a region where the true vibration wants to move smoothly, forcing the local basis to spend many modes approximating that smooth crossing. When partitions are staggered, a bad boundary in one partition becomes an interior region in another, so the missing behavior can appear as an easier substructure mode elsewhere. Combining modes from several cuts therefore gives the reduced solve more useful directions. The low-frequency interface replacement works because large-scale vibration modes are usually dominated by broad motion across boundaries, not every tiny boundary oscillation. The abstract's three-order-of-magnitude accuracy improvement is consistent with this cause: the method is not merely adding more local detail; it is adding better-shaped building blocks. It also keeps communication low because the expensive boundary information is compressed before being shared across computing ranks.
106.po: The payoff is a faster and more accurate route to large-scale modal analysis. The abstract reports three orders of magnitude better accuracy than typical Component Mode Synthesis methods, along with better strong and weak scaling in time and memory. It also preserves important practical advantages of CMS: local updates can be fast, and communication between MPI ranks can remain low. That matters when vibration analysis is too large for one machine and must run on distributed clusters with limited memory.
106.limits: The abstract does not specify which geometries, materials, or boundary conditions were tested, so the strength of the claim is tied to the reported large-scale modal analysis experiments. The method assumes useful additional motion directions can be obtained from multiple staggered partitions, and that low-frequency interface approximations are enough for the target modes. If a problem's important behavior lives in fine boundary detail, the compression may be less effective. The abstract reports scaling and accuracy gains, but not every possible partition choice or failure case.

107.bp: A statistical chart has a strict job: its lengths, areas, angles, or positions must stand for numbers. A pictorial chart adds another job: the marks should look like meaningful objects or textures that fit a story, such as themed icons or illustrated surfaces. The problem exists because these two jobs can fight. A generated picture may be attractive while quietly changing the data, and a precise chart may fail to hold attention. This paper treats the chart as neither a plain drawing nor a free image prompt. It treats it as a picture that must obey two kinds of evidence at the same time: a text prompt that describes the intended meaning, and a context image that carries the original chart's structure. The goal is automatic pictorial charts that remain faithful to the statistics.
107.wh: The hard part is that visual appeal is flexible while data structure is not. If a bar represents twice another value, the viewer must still see that relationship after the bar becomes a stack of themed objects or an illustrated form. A simple image generator can invent appealing textures, but it has no natural reason to preserve the exact chart layout. A simple chart renderer preserves layout, but it does not know how to turn a data mark into expressive imagery. The abstract names four visual channels: length, area, angle, and position. Each channel encodes numbers differently, so the system must protect different kinds of structure. Changing the height of a bar, the area of a symbol, or the angle of a slice can change the meaning. The method therefore needs separate pressure for what the chart says and where the chart's measured parts must stay.
107.naive: A smart beginner might render a normal chart and then ask an image-editing model to make it look like a theme. That can fail because the model may bend bars, resize icons, shift positions, or blur the marks that carry the numbers. Another beginner might paste pictorial textures into the existing chart shapes. That protects the layout but often looks mechanical, because the texture does not understand the semantic scene requested by the prompt. The abstract argues against treating charts merely as images to be stylized. The missing idea is that the generator must be guided by both the statistical skeleton and the intended visual meaning during image creation, not after the fact.
107.ap: The paper's central move is dual conditioning. One control signal is language: a prompt that captures the semantic context of the edit, meaning the objects, materials, or theme the viewer should recognize. The other control signal is an image of the source chart, which supplies the global structure: where marks sit and how their visual sizes or positions encode data. These signals guide a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer, a learned image generator that repeatedly turns visual noise into a cleaner image while attending to more than one kind of input. The authors add two feature-level mechanisms. Structural alignment anchors the generated image to the chart layout. Semantic alignment transfers expressive textures from reference images. This separates the task into preserving measured form and adding meaningful appearance, so the output can be pictorial without abandoning the chart's data role.
107.mech: The input is an abstract statistical chart, a text prompt describing the intended theme or editing goal, and reference imagery for expressive texture. The context chart is used as the structural guide. During generation, the model keeps internal image features, which are intermediate descriptions of shapes, positions, and textures rather than final pixels. Structural alignment acts on those features so the generated marks remain tied to the source chart's global arrangement. If the original chart encodes a value by length, the generated form must respect that length relationship; if it encodes by area, angle, or position, the corresponding spatial relationship must remain visible. Semantic alignment works in parallel. It pulls appearance cues from reference images so the marks can carry recognizable texture or pictorial meaning related to the prompt. The diffusion process then iteratively refines the output, balancing these two controls at each stage instead of applying decoration only at the end. The output is a pictorial chart. The abstract says the method generalizes across major visual channels and diverse semantic domains, and that quantitative evaluations plus perceptual user studies compare it favorably against controllable generation and image-editing baselines.
107.math: The mathematical idea is constraint balancing in a learned image-making process. A chart is a set of geometric measurements: positions, lengths, areas, and angles. Those quantities are not decorative; they are the data. The generator also has a semantic target, which is less exact: the picture should look like the requested theme. Diffusion, explained plainly, starts from a disordered image and takes many small corrective steps toward images that resemble examples while obeying the given controls. A Transformer is a pattern-matching machine that can let different parts of the input attend to one another, so words, chart regions, and image features can influence the same output. Alignment means making two internal descriptions agree. Structural alignment reduces wrongness in layout: generated marks should occupy the places and proportions implied by the chart. Semantic alignment reduces wrongness in meaning: textures and visual details should match the prompt and references. The tradeoff is expressiveness versus measurement faithfulness. The math fits because the output must satisfy soft but simultaneous pressures, not a single hand-written drawing rule for every possible chart theme and visual channel.
107.dots: This paper connects to generative image work, but its deeper problem is visualization: pictures must communicate numbers without lying about them. It sits near controllable generation because the model is steered by external signals rather than a prompt alone. It also connects to reconstruction and editing papers that preserve structure while changing appearance. In graphics terms, it resembles material and texture transfer, except the protected object is not a 3D surface; it is the measured geometry of a chart. It also neighbors user-facing design tools, where the hard question is how much automation can be allowed before control is lost. The repeated SIGGRAPH theme is separation of roles: keep a structural backbone fixed enough to remain trustworthy, then give a generative process room to fill in detail, texture, and semantic style.
107.ww: The mechanism should work better than plain stylization because it gives the model a reason to protect the data-bearing structure while it invents appearance. If a generator sees only a text prompt, it can satisfy the prompt by moving chart marks into a more pleasing composition, which damages the numbers. If it sees only the chart, it may produce a faithful but visually plain result. Feeding both signals and enforcing alignment inside the model gives each generation step access to both goals. Structural alignment keeps the spatial skeleton from drifting. Semantic alignment keeps the decorative layer from becoming arbitrary by tying it to reference appearance and text intent. The abstract's claim of success across length, area, angle, and position matters because each channel can break in a different way. A method that handles several channels is less likely to be only a bar-chart trick.
107.po: The payoff is automated pictorial chart creation that aims to be both memorable and data-faithful. The abstract reports stronger quantitative results and perceptual user-study results than traditional controllable generation and image-editing baselines. It also claims coverage across length, area, angle, and position, which means the method is not limited to one chart geometry. For visual storytelling, that buys a way to make expressive charts without manually redrawing every graphic or trusting unconstrained image editing to preserve numbers and layout clearly.
107.limits: The abstract does not provide the exact datasets, metrics, or examples beyond broad claims, and the project page text is truncated. The method assumes the source chart's global structure can be read from a context image and that the prompt and reference images describe a compatible pictorial treatment. It also assumes alignment in feature space is enough to preserve statistical faithfulness. The abstract reports user studies, but it does not prove that every generated chart will be safe for high-stakes communication without human checking.

108.bp: Many 3D systems describe a surface indirectly. Instead of storing triangles immediately, they store a function that answers a simple question at any point in space: how far am I from the nearest surface? An unsigned distance function gives only the distance, not whether the point is inside or outside. That is useful for reconstruction and shape generation because it can describe difficult surfaces, including places where sheets meet or cross in ways that do not form a clean solid. But most graphics tools still need a triangle surface at the end. DCx is about extracting that surface from a neural unsigned distance function. The practical problem is turning smooth distance answers into connected triangles while preserving the intended surface arrangement, especially in non-manifold regions, meaning places where the surface is not a simple two-sided skin.
108.wh: The usual extraction method, Dual Contouring, was built for signed distance functions. A signed distance says not only how far a point is from the surface, but also which side of the surface it is on. That sign gives a strong clue: if neighboring grid corners have different signs, the surface must pass between them. Unsigned distance removes that clue. Every value is nonnegative, so there is no sign flip to mark an active cube. A naive detector can miss surface pieces or create false ones. Non-manifold structures add another problem. When sheets touch, branch, or fold into locally unusual arrangements, a rule that expects one clean surface through each grid cube can connect triangles incorrectly. The abstract says standard active-cube detection becomes unreliable and connections can fail in such regions.
108.naive: A beginner might adapt signed-distance extraction by choosing a small distance threshold: if a grid cube contains points close enough to the surface, mark it active and place triangles there. This can fail because closeness alone does not say how the surface crosses the cube or which nearby pieces should connect. Another attempt would be to run standard Dual Contouring anyway, but it depends on sign changes that unsigned fields do not provide. For non-manifold cases, one vertex per active cube can be too little local information. Different sheets may pass through the same neighborhood, and forcing them into the wrong single connection pattern can change the shape's intended structure.
108.ap: DCx modifies Dual Contouring so it no longer relies on inside-outside signs. Instead of operating on only individual grid cubes, it looks at expanded cubes, each a 2 by 2 by 2 block of voxels. That gives the method more local context around a possible surface crossing. For deciding which cubes are active, it uses an optimization-based strategy: it searches for a choice of active regions that better matches the unsigned distance evidence than a simple sign-change rule could. For connection recovery, it introduces a voxel-to-mesh lookup table, where mesh means the triangle surface being extracted. The table stores triangle connection templates for local voxel configurations. Once the local configuration is known, the method can use a predefined pattern to create triangles, including patterns that handle non-manifold surface arrangements.
108.mech: The input is a neural unsigned distance function sampled over a voxel grid. Each voxel is a small box-shaped cell in space, and the function can be queried to estimate distance to the nearest surface. DCx first needs to decide where the hidden zero-level set is, meaning the places where the distance should be zero and therefore where the surface lies. Because there are no signs, it uses an optimization-based active-cube decision rather than checking sign flips. It then groups neighboring cells into expanded cubes, 2 by 2 by 2 voxel blocks, so each local decision sees more than one cell at a time. For each local voxel configuration, the method consults a lookup table that maps that configuration to a triangle connection pattern. This avoids inventing connectivity from scratch for every case. The table says which extracted vertices should be connected into edges and faces. The output is a triangle surface extracted from the distance representation. The abstract says these changes avoid failures from unreliable active-cube detection and correct connections in non-manifold regions, allowing both manifold and non-manifold surfaces to be extracted.
108.math: The underlying mathematical object is a level set: a surface defined as all points where a function has a particular value. Here the value is zero distance from the surface. With signed distance, the function changes from negative to positive across the surface, so a sign change brackets the crossing. With unsigned distance, the function only dips to zero and rises again, so the crossing is more like finding the bottom of a valley than finding where a road crosses a border. That is why active-cube selection becomes an optimization problem. Optimization, unpacked here, means choosing active cubes so the extracted surface best agrees with the distance values and local arrangement. Expanded cubes add neighborhood context, which is a geometric idea: a surface connection cannot always be inferred from one cell alone. The lookup table is discrete mathematics. It turns many possible local yes-no voxel configurations into known triangle templates. The tradeoff is flexibility versus reliability: templates limit local choices, but they prevent many inconsistent hand-made decisions in difficult configurations and make extraction repeatable across neighboring cells of the grid.
108.dots: DCx sits in the geometry-processing and neural-representation part of SIGGRAPH. It connects to reconstruction because neural fields often predict continuous shape evidence before a usable surface exists. It connects to mesh-generation work such as Nexus because both papers care about the same hidden issue: a 3D shape is not only a set of points; its connections determine whether tools can use it. It also relates to coordinate and sampling ideas. The distance function is an alternate coordinate-like description of the shape, and the voxel grid samples that description in space. The broader recurring problem is conversion: one representation is convenient for learning or reconstruction, while another is needed for rendering, editing, or fabrication. DCx focuses on making that conversion preserve difficult surface structures rather than smoothing them into simpler solids.
108.ww: The method should improve over standard Dual Contouring because it replaces the missing sign evidence with decisions based on the evidence that still exists: unsigned distances and local voxel patterns. Looking at expanded cubes gives enough neighborhood context to distinguish cases that would look ambiguous inside a single cube. That matters especially where surfaces touch or branch, because local connectivity depends on nearby samples. The lookup table helps for a causal reason: once a local configuration is recognized, the triangle pattern can be chosen consistently instead of recomputed by a fragile rule. This reduces wrong connections in non-manifold regions. The approach also remains efficient because table lookup is cheap after the active regions are found. The abstract's claim that DCx is conceptually simple and easy to implement follows from this structure: optimize activation, classify local configuration, apply a template carefully.
108.po: The payoff is practical extraction of triangle surfaces from neural unsigned distance functions, including both ordinary two-sided surfaces and non-manifold structures. The abstract says DCx improves on Dual Contouring by avoiding unreliable active-cube detection and correcting connections in difficult regions. It also says the method is simple and efficient through predefined templates. For 3D reconstruction and generation, that buys a cleaner bridge from a learned distance representation to the triangle surfaces used by downstream graphics tools and editing systems later.
108.limits: The abstract is truncated after saying experiments show that, so the exact measured results and comparisons are not visible here. The method assumes the unsigned distance function is accurate enough for active-cube decisions and that local voxel configurations fit the lookup table's cases. Grid resolution will matter, because tiny structures can be missed if the sampled cells are too coarse. The abstract claims support for non-manifold surfaces, but it does not reveal all pathological cases or the cost of building and using the templates.

109.bp: Virtual try-on for 3D assets asks a practical production question: can a garment made for one body be put automatically onto a very different character? In real asset libraries, clothing and characters rarely share the same skeleton, body template, pose, point count, or point-to-point correspondence. A jacket, robot body, cartoon figure, and human scan may all describe shape differently. The work in this abstract aims to make clothing reusable at large scale by dressing complex, multi-layer garments onto diverse posed humanoids. The visible goal is plausible drape: the garment should wrap, hang, and fit around the target rather than merely being copied into the same space. The paper's key organizing idea is to use SMPL, a standard human body model, as an intermediate proxy so garments and target bodies can meet through a common reference.
109.wh: The hard part is correspondence: deciding which place on one shape should match which place on another. For clothing, this is especially difficult because the garment may cover only part of the body, may have layers, and may have complex connectivity, including non-manifold triangle surfaces where sheets and seams do not behave like a simple clean shell. The target body may also vary greatly in pose, shape, and style. If a shirt was built around a human body and the target is a stylized cartoon or robot, there may be no obvious direct map. Even after correspondence is found, the garment cannot just be glued onto the body. Cloth-like objects need to settle under physical constraints, avoiding impossible intersections and producing believable draping. The abstract separates these pressures into partial-to-complete alignment for clothing and large pose, shape, and style variation for bodies.
109.naive: A beginner might scale the garment until it surrounds the target body, then snap nearby garment points to nearby body points. This fails when the target pose differs, when the body has different proportions, or when nearest points are semantically wrong, such as a sleeve matching the torso. Another simple attempt would require every garment and character to share the same template and dense correspondences. The abstract says real-world assets rarely satisfy that condition. A third attempt would transfer the garment geometry and stop there, but then folds and collisions may be physically implausible. The missing pieces are a shared reference body, reliable correspondences across style changes, and a fitting step that lets the garment settle.
109.ap: The method uses SMPL as a middle body that both sides can relate to. Instead of solving garment-to-target directly, it decomposes transfer into two correspondence tasks. Clothing-to-SMPL handles partial-to-complete alignment: a garment covers only some body regions, so the system must infer how that partial object relates to the full proxy body. The abstract says this part uses a geometry-driven correspondence model. Body-to-SMPL handles the target character, where pose, shape, and stylization can vary widely. For this, the paper uses a diffusion-based correspondence approach, meaning a learned iterative process for producing matches, guided by multi-view consistent appearance features and a pretrained 2D foundation model. Once correspondences are available, the system registers SMPL and SMPL+D, a displaced version of the body proxy, to the garment and target, then transfers the garment through a smooth SMPL-to-SMPL+D transition with simulator-driven fitting.
109.mech: The inputs are a source garment, possibly complex and multi-layered, and a target humanoid in an arbitrary pose. The system first relates the garment to SMPL. Because the garment is partial, it cannot match every body region, so the geometry-driven model must identify which body areas the clothing corresponds to and how its shape sits relative to the proxy. Next, the target body is related back to SMPL. This stage must handle large changes in pose, body shape, and visual style. The abstract says it uses multi-view consistent appearance features, so evidence from several views is combined in a way that agrees across cameras, and a pretrained 2D foundation model, which supplies general image understanding learned before this task. A diffusion-based process produces body-to-SMPL correspondences. With both maps, the method registers SMPL or SMPL+D to the garment and the target body. SMPL+D adds displacement, meaning extra surface offsets beyond the plain proxy. The garment is then moved along a smooth path from SMPL toward SMPL+D and finally fitted by a simulator, which adjusts the cloth-like shape under physical constraints. The output is a dressed target character, and the abstract also says clothing size can be customized quickly after draping.
109.math: The main mathematical idea is composing correspondences through an intermediate space. A correspondence is a map saying that this point or region on one shape matches that point or region on another. Direct garment-to-character mapping is hard because the two shapes may have different structures. By mapping garment to SMPL and target body to SMPL, the system uses SMPL as a shared coordinate system. The geometry-driven stage relies on spatial relationships such as nearby surfaces, coverage, and shape compatibility. The diffusion stage uses learned generation: it starts from uncertain matches and repeatedly refines them toward correspondences that agree with multi-view appearance and the pretrained image model's features. Registration is another mathematical move: adjust the proxy shape so it aligns with observed garment or body geometry. The simulator-driven fitting then solves physical constraints, such as cloth not occupying the same space as the body and draping smoothly. The tradeoff is universality versus exact identity. SMPL simplifies matching across assets, but it is still a proxy, so the method must use displacement and fitting to recover detail that the proxy cannot store.
109.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of geometry, animation, capture, and physical simulation. Like the Nexus and DCx papers, it treats triangle-surface connectivity as a practical obstacle, but here the deeper issue is reuse: existing assets must work together despite incompatible construction histories. It also connects to generative diffusion methods because learned iterative refinement is used for correspondence under large variation, not only for making pictures or shapes. The simulator-driven fitting links it to cloth and physical animation, where final believability depends on contact and drape rather than pure geometric matching. More broadly, it follows a common SIGGRAPH pattern: introduce an intermediate representation that makes a wild matching problem manageable, then use physical or geometric correction to restore details that the simplification would otherwise lose.
109.ww: The approach should work because it avoids the most brittle direct match. A garment and a stylized target body may have little obvious point-to-point agreement, but both can be related to a human-like proxy. That turns one hard correspondence into two more structured ones. The clothing-to-SMPL model can focus on partial coverage, while the body-to-SMPL model can focus on pose, shape, and style. Multi-view appearance features help because a single view can hide body parts or confuse front and back, while several consistent views provide stronger evidence. The pretrained 2D model contributes broad visual recognition that may transfer across humans, robots, cartoons, and other humanoid characters, as claimed in the abstract. The simulator matters after matching because a correct map is not the same as a wearable drape. Physical fitting can repair intersections and let the garment settle around the target.
109.po: The payoff is automated reuse of real-world 3D garments across diverse humanoid characters. The abstract claims the system handles complex multi-layer garments, complex garment connectivity, and targets including humans, robots, cartoons, and creatures while staying computationally practical. It also supports fast clothing-size customization after draping. For production, the value is reducing the manual work of retargeting clothes while keeping the output physically plausible enough to be useful in asset libraries and character pipelines for repeated production use across many assets.
109.limits: The abstract is truncated before completing its final evidence sentence, so exact evaluation details are not available here. The method assumes the characters are humanoid enough for SMPL to serve as a useful bridge. It also depends on good multi-view appearance features, useful pretrained 2D features, and a simulator that can fit the transferred garment without creating unacceptable artifacts. Very unusual bodies, garments that do not correspond to human clothing regions, or poor input geometry may fall outside what the abstract proves.

110.bp: Hand-drawn image styles are not only about which objects are visible. A line drawing, a hatch pattern, or a halftone dot pattern also has a layout on the final page. Lines should stay attached to meaningful visual features, and tone marks should behave like a coherent image pattern, even when the picture is made by tracing light through reflections, shadows, and other indirect paths. The paper is trying to join two worlds that usually pull apart. One world is image-space style, where marks are placed on the flat picture. The other is path-space light transport, where a pixel is explained by many possible routes that light could take through the scene. Recent stylized rendering equations let style interact with those light routes, but the abstract says they do not enforce image-space consistency. This work asks how a style designed on the picture can be carried into the light-path calculation without losing the visual structure that makes it read as drawing.
110.wh: The difficulty is that a drawn mark lives in the finished image, while the rendering calculation lives along paths through the scene. A single pixel may receive light through several bounces, blurry reflections, depth of field, or other distribution effects. If a style is applied only after the image is formed, it may ignore how light actually arrived. If the style is applied only along light paths, it may lose the page-level arrangement that makes hatching or feature lines look intentional. The obvious bridge is unstable because there is not one simple path for every image mark. A line seen in the picture may correspond to many nearby geometric situations, and a tone pattern on the image must be evaluated at places along paths that are not themselves pixels. The paper therefore needs a way to map flat image structure into path space while preserving the structure that the viewer recognizes.
110.naive: A smart beginner might render a physically shaded image first and then draw lines, hatching, or halftone dots on top of the final pixels. That preserves the flat image pattern, but it treats style as paint pasted after the light calculation. It cannot naturally follow soft shadows, reflections, or other effects that arise from paths through the scene. Another beginner might attach style rules directly to rays or surface hits. That lets style participate in the light calculation, but the marks can lose their image-space agreement: a hatch field may not line up as a coherent drawing, or a feature line may behave differently under distribution effects than it would in the final picture.
110.ap: The core move is to lift image-space stylization into path space. In plain terms, the paper builds mappings from points and structures in the flat picture to corresponding places along light paths, and those mappings are driven by scene geometry. For feature lines, it uses a conditional lifting based on partial path-space variation. The abstract says a geometric path description is combined with parallel transport, which means carrying a direction or local frame along a path while keeping it as consistent as the geometry allows. This is meant to preserve image structure under distribution effects. For tone styles such as hatching and halftone, the paper proposes a canonical lifting anchored to a material-independent mapping. The abstract connects that mapping to stationary-phase arguments from wave optics, so the tone field can be evaluated at path vertices rather than only at final pixels.
110.mech: The input is an image-space style, such as feature lines or a tone field, plus the scene and the light paths used by the stylized rendering equation. The mechanism first asks what kind of style is being carried. For feature lines, the system studies how a light path changes when the underlying geometry changes. It uses partial variation in path space to decide where line evidence should live. A geometric path description gives coordinates for nearby path changes, and parallel transport carries local image structure through those changes so that the line is not redefined from scratch at every path sample. The resulting line detection is curvature-aware, meaning it responds to how the surface bends, and stochastic, meaning it works inside a sampling process rather than requiring every possible path to be known. For tone styles, the system builds a more canonical mapping that does not depend on material identity. The abstract says this is motivated by stationary-phase reasoning from wave optics: the important contributions are tied to places where small changes do not rapidly cancel the signal. A locally invertible approximation then lets the renderer ask, at an arbitrary point along a path, which location in the image-space tone field should be read. The output is a path-space style evaluation that still respects image-space structure.
110.math: The main mathematical idea is a change of address. Image-space uses two-dimensional addresses on the final picture. Path-space uses higher-dimensional addresses that describe a chain of events: camera point, surface hits, directions, and light interaction. A mapping says how an address in one world corresponds to an address in the other. That fits the paper because the desired drawing style begins as a flat pattern, but the rendering process needs values along paths. For lines, the abstract names partial path-space variation, which means measuring how selected parts of a path change when geometry or viewing conditions move. It also names parallel transport, the rule for carrying a local direction across a curved setting without introducing extra twisting. This matters because a line or hatch direction should not spin arbitrarily as it moves through the path calculation. Curvature supplies another idea: bends in the surface create visual features, so the method looks for line evidence in the way nearby geometry changes. For tone, stationary phase is the idea that rapidly oscillating contributions often cancel except near special stable places. The tradeoff is consistency versus physical participation: the style must stay coherent as a picture while still entering the light-path sum.
110.dots: This paper sits between non-photorealistic rendering and light transport. It connects to rendering work that treats an image as the sum of many sampled light paths, because the style is evaluated inside that path calculation rather than only after it. It also connects to geometry work, because feature lines are tied to surface shape, curvature, and how paths vary when the scene changes. A third neighbor is coordinate-change work: the paper is mostly about moving a pattern from one coordinate world, the image plane, into another coordinate world, the space of light paths, while preserving what the viewer sees as consistent. The abstract also links tone to wave optics, where tiny waves can cancel or reinforce. The shared SIGGRAPH problem is how to keep artistic control without breaking the physical or geometric structure that makes an image believable.
110.ww: The method should improve over the naive approaches because it gives the style the right place to live. A post-process drawing filter sees only finished pixels, so it cannot know why the pixel received its color. A path-only style rule sees light transport, but it may forget the flat picture organization that hand-drawn styles depend on. By building geometry-driven mappings, the paper gives every path sample a way to ask where it belongs in the original image-style field. For feature lines, carrying local structure by parallel transport reduces arbitrary changes in direction when paths pass through curved or distributed effects. For tone, a material-independent mapping avoids tying hatching or halftone layout to one surface label, and the local inverse lets the renderer evaluate the tone field at path vertices. The result is causal: the style participates in lighting because it is read during path evaluation, yet it remains recognizable because its image-space address system is preserved.
110.po: The payoff is a principled way to make image-based drawing styles interact with light transport. The abstract demonstrates the idea for feature lines and for tone styles such as hatching and halftone. For lines, it claims a curvature-aware, stochastic, geometry-driven formulation that generalizes earlier ray-based methods. For tone, it gives a way to evaluate image-space tone fields at arbitrary path vertices. This buys a renderer that can treat line and tone styles as part of the path-space calculation while keeping the consistency inherited from hand-drawn media.
110.limits: The abstract is cut off at the end, so the exact final claim and full evaluation details are not visible in the input. The method assumes that useful geometry-driven mappings from image-space to path-space can be established. It also relies on approximations: the tone lifting uses a locally invertible approximation, so it may fail where the mapping stops behaving locally like a reversible address change. For feature lines, the abstract supports claims about curvature-aware stochastic line detection, but it does not prove from the visible text how every drawing style, material, or distribution effect behaves.

111.bp: A 3D scene can contain visible outlines, material borders, contour curves, and other lines that an artist or tool wants to turn into a clean 2D vector drawing. The useful output is not just a pile of strokes. It should be a flat map divided into solid shaded regions, with occlusion handled so that hidden parts do not incorrectly cut visible regions. This matters for illustration, technical drawing, stylized rendering, and editing, because vector images are expected to have clean regions that can be filled, selected, and changed. The paper starts from curves derived from 3D geometry and produces a planar map, meaning a subdivision of the image plane into connected cells. Its central concern is reliability: the input curves may come from many kinds of surfaces, and the curve pieces may not meet perfectly. The method aims to produce a valid 2D partition even when the curve collection is messy.
111.wh: The hard part is that curves in a projected 3D scene do not arrive as a perfectly assembled drawing. Some curves cross, some stop near one another without sharing an endpoint, some are hidden by closer surfaces, and some have mathematical forms that are hard to intersect exactly. A simple region-building algorithm needs to know every crossing and connection. If it misses one intersection, a filled area can leak into the wrong place. If it invents a connection, two separate regions can merge. General curve-curve intersection is especially fragile because both curves can bend, and tiny numerical errors can change the answer near tangencies or nearly touching endpoints. The paper also wants to accept curves from polygonal, NURBS, or subdivision surfaces and output arbitrary curve segment types. That flexibility makes it harder to rely on a single special case. The method must scale to many primitives without requiring perfect input.
111.naive: A beginner would collect all visible curves, compute every pairwise curve-curve intersection, split the curves at those crossings, connect matching endpoints, and then trace the enclosed regions. This is the natural textbook route. It fails when the input is curve soup: endpoints that should meet are not explicitly connected, and numerical error leaves tiny gaps or overlaps. It also becomes expensive when many curves are present, because testing every pair wastes work on curves that are far apart. Even when acceleration structures are added, the final planar map still has to survive uncertain intersections, approximate arithmetic, and curves of many types.
111.ap: The paper's key observation is that the spatial hierarchy used to accelerate intersection tests can also become the planar map itself. Instead of treating the hierarchy as a temporary search aid and then building a separate exact curve arrangement, the method lets the cells of that hierarchy define the regions of the flat picture. A spatial hierarchy divides the image into boxes or cells, so curve relationships are resolved locally. This replaces difficult general curve-curve intersection with simpler curve-line intersection, because curves are mostly tested against cell boundaries. The user can choose a precision, and the method resolves intersections only up to that precision. Because the cells form a well-defined subdivision even when curve endpoints do not explicitly connect, the output remains a valid planar map rather than a broken collection of almost-connected strokes.
111.mech: The input is a collection of curves derived from the 3D scene: silhouettes, isolines, material boundaries, and similar visual separators. The method first accounts for proper occlusion, so the 2D drawing describes what should be visible from the chosen view. It then organizes the image plane with a spatial hierarchy, a nested division of the plane into cells. Curves are inserted into this hierarchy, and the same structure that says which curves might meet in a region also stores the regions of the final map. When the algorithm needs local intersections, it avoids solving arbitrary curve against arbitrary curve wherever possible. It asks where a curve crosses the straight boundary of a cell, a simpler and more stable question. The cells become the basic pieces of the planar map. If the input has endpoints that nearly meet but are not explicitly connected, the containing cells still give the algorithm a definite subdivision to work with. The user-defined precision controls how finely the hierarchy is refined. Work is therefore output-sensitive: the algorithm spends effort where the requested drawing detail requires it, not everywhere. The output is a 2D vector image whose plane is partitioned into solid shaded regions and whose curve segments may have arbitrary parametric form.
111.math: The central mathematical object is a planar map: a flat surface divided by curves into cells, edges, and vertices. The important requirement is consistency. Every cell must know its boundary, every boundary must separate neighboring cells, and the filled regions must not depend on accidental gaps. The paper uses a spatial hierarchy, which is a repeated subdivision of the plane into simpler pieces. This is a coordinate and scale idea: instead of solving the entire drawing at once, the plane is broken into local boxes where simpler decisions can be made. Curve-line intersection is the main simplification. A bent curve against another bent curve can have complicated near misses and tangencies, but a bent curve against a straight cell boundary is easier to locate and easier to bound numerically. The user-defined precision introduces a controlled approximation: the result is not trying to discover infinitely exact crossings; it is trying to produce a valid drawing at the requested resolution. The tradeoff is exact geometric detail versus dependable region structure. By letting hierarchy cells define the map, the method protects the combinatorial part, meaning the record of what touches what, from small numerical errors.
111.dots: This paper connects to geometry processing because it turns 3D scene features into a clean 2D structure while preserving occlusion. It connects to vector graphics because the output is not pixels but editable curve-bounded regions. It also connects to the broader SIGGRAPH theme of replacing a brittle exact problem with a structured approximation that keeps the relationships users care about. Neighboring rendering papers ask how light reaches the image; this paper asks how visible geometric separators become a usable drawing. Neighboring fabrication and modeling papers also care about valid partitions and connection patterns, because downstream tools often fail when a shape is almost but not quite connected. Here, the shared problem is not visual realism. It is making a representation that remains well-defined under imperfect input and finite arithmetic.
111.ww: The method works for the same reason a city map remains usable when details are drawn at a chosen scale. If every boundary is forced to live inside a cell structure, the map has a definite set of regions even before every microscopic curve relation is settled. Replacing curve-curve tests with curve-line tests removes a major source of fragility, because the algorithm repeatedly asks a simpler question against known cell boundaries. The hierarchy also naturally avoids unnecessary work: distant curves live in different cells, and fine decisions are only needed where curves crowd together or where the requested precision demands refinement. For curve soup, the cell structure supplies missing organization. A tiny endpoint mismatch no longer has to decide whether the whole filled region leaks, because the planar map is defined by the hierarchy. This explains how the approach can be both flexible across curve types and dependable in the presence of numerical error.
111.po: The output is a 2D vector image that partitions the image plane into solid shaded regions while respecting occlusion from the 3D scene. The abstract says the method handles curves from polygonal, NURBS, and subdivision surfaces, and it supports output curve segments of arbitrary parametric type. It also says the method scales to many primitives and resolves intersections only up to a user-defined precision while preserving a valid planar map. The practical gain is a cleaner bridge from complex 3D scene curves to editable 2D vector artwork.
111.limits: The abstract is cut off near the evaluation claim, so the exact measured efficiency statement is incomplete in the input. The method assumes the user can choose a precision that is appropriate for the intended output. Very fine detail below that scale may be deliberately collapsed or approximated. The paper promises proper occlusion, but the visible abstract does not describe the full visibility computation or its failure cases. The approach also depends on the spatial hierarchy being refined enough where curves crowd together; otherwise the map is valid at the chosen scale but may not match every tiny geometric distinction.

112.bp: An image can be stored as a grid of pixels, but that is not always the best way to compress, edit, or learn it. Many images contain broad regions, sharp boundaries, elongated strokes, and repeated local structure. A representation that knows which part of the image owns which pixels can describe such structure more compactly than treating every pixel as unrelated. This paper introduces Soft Anisotropic Diagrams, or SAD, as an explicit image representation made from adaptive sites placed in the image plane. A site is a small owner or anchor that contributes color to nearby pixels. Unlike a rigid square pixel block, each site can have a direction-sensitive distance rule, so it can stretch its influence along an edge or texture. The goal is to render images efficiently while still allowing learning signals to move sites, boundaries, and colors into better positions. The result is a picture built from soft local ownership rather than a fixed grid alone.
112.wh: The hard part is balancing clarity, speed, and learnability. If each pixel is stored directly, rendering is simple but compression and structure are poor. If an image is described by larger regions, it can be compact, but sharp edges and fine details become hard to place. If ownership is completely hard, a pixel belongs to exactly one site, then small boundary changes can cause sudden jumps that are difficult to learn from. If ownership is too soft, boundaries blur and the image loses crisp structure. The paper also wants fixed-size local computation on a GPU, so each pixel cannot compare itself to every site in the image. A practical method must decide which few sites matter for each pixel, keep useful learning signals near boundaries, and update the site set as the image demands more or less detail.
112.naive: A beginner might place many colored dots over the image and color each pixel from the nearest dot. That creates a simple region diagram, but the regions are too round and blunt for elongated edges. Another attempt would blend from all dots, which gives smooth learning signals but is too expensive and can wash out boundaries. A third attempt would use a fixed number of sites everywhere, but images do not spend detail evenly: a flat wall needs few anchors, while text, edges, or texture need more. These simple choices fail because they do not let ownership be directional, adaptive, local, and learnable at the same time.
112.ap: SAD gives each site a richer way to claim pixels. Instead of measuring ordinary circular distance, each site specifies an anisotropic metric, meaning distance can stretch differently in different directions, plus an added weight that shifts its influence. Pixel color is computed as a softmax blend over only a small top-K set of nearby candidate sites. Softmax means larger scores dominate while smaller scores still contribute enough to provide a learning signal. The resulting partition is a softened version of a weighted Voronoi diagram, where the image is divided according to nearest owners, but with direction-sensitive shapes and learnable softness. The method keeps a per-query top-K map so each pixel only considers a fixed small list. It updates those lists through a propagation scheme inspired by jump flooding, with random injection to avoid missing distant but relevant sites.
112.mech: The input is an image to encode. The method begins by placing adaptive sites in the image plane, with initialization guided by image gradients, meaning it pays attention to places where color changes strongly. Each site stores color-related information, a direction-sensitive distance rule, an added weight, and a temperature controlling how soft or sharp its ownership should be. For a pixel, the renderer does not inspect all sites. It keeps a top-K list, the small set of sites currently believed to matter most under the same shading score used to color the pixel. The pixel evaluates those candidates, turns their scores into softmax weights, and blends their colors. During training, the difference between the rendered image and the target image produces signals that adjust site positions, distance shapes, weights, temperatures, and colors through Adam, an iterative adjustment method that uses recent error directions to choose steps. The top-K map is updated by propagation inspired by jump flooding: good candidates spread across neighboring pixels quickly. Stochastic injection, a small amount of random candidate insertion, gives possible global coverage so the method can recover if a faraway site should matter. Adaptive budget control adds sites where more detail is needed and prunes sites that are not useful. The output is a compact, explicit image description and a rendered image from that description.
112.math: The first mathematical idea is a distance diagram. Put sites on a plane, define a distance from every pixel to every site, and let the closest sites explain the pixel. A Voronoi diagram is the hard version of this idea: each location belongs to its nearest site. SAD uses an additively weighted anisotropic version. Additive weights let a site act larger or smaller than raw distance would suggest. Anisotropy means direction matters: distance can be cheap along one direction and expensive across another, which fits edges and strokes better than circular influence. The second idea is soft ownership. Softmax turns scores into positive weights that sum to one, so a pixel can mostly belong to one site while still receiving learning signals from nearby competitors. The third idea is local approximation. Comparing every pixel to every site is too costly, so the method keeps only a top-K candidate set. The tradeoff is global exactness versus fast fixed-size computation. Propagation and random injection manage that tradeoff by spreading likely candidates locally while occasionally testing broader alternatives. Learning is the repeated adjustment of numbers to reduce visible difference from the target image.
112.dots: This paper connects to neural image representation because it learns a compact structure that can reproduce an image, but it stays explicit: sites, distances, ownership, and colors are concrete objects in the image plane. It connects to geometry because the representation divides a plane into regions, much like planar maps and weighted cell diagrams. It also connects to GPU rendering, where fixed-size local work is valuable because thousands of pixels can run the same small computation in parallel. A neighboring SIGGRAPH idea is sampling: the top-K list is a choice about which sites are worth spending computation on. Another is reconstruction: the image is recovered from fewer structured pieces rather than stored as independent pixels. The broader theme is compact storage versus faithful recovery, with boundaries being the hardest place to get both.
112.ww: SAD should work better than the naive dot-owner scheme because its sites are shaped and softened in ways that match images. Direction-sensitive distance lets a site cover an elongated edge without needing many small round regions. Added weights let ownership shift without moving the site itself. Learnable temperatures let the method decide whether a boundary should be sharp or blended. The top-K map makes the computation practical: most pixels only need the few owners that can plausibly affect them. Propagation works because neighboring pixels usually have similar nearest sites, so a good candidate for one pixel is often useful nearby. Random injection handles the exception, where a local update path misses a better site elsewhere. Densification and pruning make the budget follow the picture, adding capacity where error remains and removing unused anchors. The causal reason is that the representation gives the image both region ownership and smooth adjustment paths, so training can move toward clear boundaries instead of fighting sudden discontinuities.
112.po: The payoff is a learned image representation that is explicit, locally computed, and aligned with image content. The abstract reports efficient rendering through per-query top-K maps and a GPU-first training pipeline. It also reports better matched-bitrate results than Image-GS and Instant-NGP on standard tests, including 46.0 dB PSNR on Kodak with 2.2 seconds encoding time, compared with 28 seconds for Image-GS, plus 4 to 19 times end-to-end training speedups over stated baselines. These numbers are from the abstract, though the visible text is cut off before the final demonstration sentence.
112.limits: The abstract is truncated, so the full list of demonstrated effects is not visible. The method assumes the image can be well explained by a finite set of adaptive sites with local top-K ownership. It may be less direct for structure that requires many distant sites to interact at once, because the fast renderer deliberately limits each pixel to a small candidate list. The top-K map is an approximation to nearest neighbors under the shading score, so errors in that list can affect quality. Reported performance is grounded in named benchmarks and baselines, but the abstract alone does not show all images, settings, or failure cases.

113.bp: Large visual-effects simulations often model things like liquid surfaces, flames, and explosions across huge volumes. No single machine may be the best place to do all that work, so the domain is split among several computers. The problem is not merely cutting space into equal boxes. The active part of the simulation can be sparse, oddly shaped, and moving quickly. A splash stretches into thin sheets, a flame front curls, and an explosion expands into empty space. If the split is poor, one computer gets too much work, or neighboring computers must exchange too much boundary data, or the split changes so abruptly over time that the whole computation becomes awkward. This paper proposes a partitioning method based on optimal transport, which means moving workload into balanced regions with minimal unnecessary displacement. The goal is even work, low communication, and stable changes over time for production-scale simulations.
113.wh: The central tension is that a good partition must satisfy several demands at once. Each node should receive a fair share of computation, because one overloaded node slows the whole simulation. Neighboring nodes should share as little boundary as possible, because data exchange across machines is expensive. The partition should also change smoothly over time, because liquids, fire, and explosions evolve every frame. A naive spatial split can look reasonable at one moment and become bad as the active region moves or changes shape. Sparse dynamic domains make this worse: much of the enclosing box may be empty, while the active material forms twisting regions. The abstract also says the domains can change shape and connection pattern rapidly. That means a method cannot assume a fixed block layout or a slowly deforming shape. It needs to repartition while keeping the artist-facing behavior intuitive.
113.naive: A beginner might divide the simulation box into equal rectangular chunks and assign one chunk to each machine. That is simple and predictable, but it wastes work when most chunks contain empty space and overloads chunks where liquid, flame, or smoke concentrates. Another attempt is to rebalance every frame based only on current workload. That can even out the work, but it may make partition boundaries jump around, increasing data movement and making temporal behavior inconsistent. A third attempt is to hand-place regions for each shot, but film production data changes too much and contains too many cases for manual splitting to be a dependable general answer.
113.ap: The paper uses optimal transport to create a power diagram for the active simulation domain. In plain language, it treats partitioning as a fair assignment problem: distribute the active computational work among centers so each center receives an appropriate amount while the total movement or mismatch is kept low. A power diagram is a weighted cell division, where each center owns a region and the weights adjust the sizes of those regions. Unlike a fixed grid, the cells can adapt to the actual shape of the active domain. The method is designed for sparse domains whose shapes change rapidly. It tries to balance three production needs: even task distribution, reduced data exchange between nodes, and temporal consistency, meaning the partition should not thrash from one frame to the next. The abstract also introduces surface index and temporal consistency index to measure those qualities.
113.mech: The input is a physics-based simulation domain from visual effects, such as free-surface liquid, flame, or explosion data. The domain is sparse and dynamic, so the method focuses on where computation actually exists rather than treating the whole enclosing volume equally. The algorithm places partition generators, which can be understood as centers that will own parts of the domain. Through optimal transport, the method adjusts the weighted ownership of those centers so that computational tasks are evenly distributed. The resulting ownership regions form a power diagram: every active point is assigned to the center that wins after distance and weight are considered. The weights allow cell sizes to change, so a center covering a dense or large part can be corrected until workload is more balanced. At the same time, the partitioner considers communication pressure, because neighboring cells need to exchange boundary information during the simulation. It also considers time: the partition at the current moment should remain consistent with nearby moments instead of completely rearranging itself. The output is a set of domain partitions assigned to compute nodes. The paper then evaluates partition quality with a surface index, tied to boundary or surface exchange, and a temporal consistency index, tied to how stable the partition is over time, using real-world film production data.
113.math: The main mathematical idea is optimal transport, the problem of moving or assigning a quantity from one arrangement to another while paying as little unnecessary cost as possible. Here the quantity is computational work spread over an active simulation domain. The partitioner wants to assign that work to nodes evenly, but not by ignoring where it sits in space. A power diagram is the geometric form that comes out: space is divided among weighted centers, and the weights let the cells grow or shrink until the assigned amounts match the desired workload. This is different from ordinary nearest-center division, where each center simply owns the closest points. The weights add a balancing handle. Partial differential equations also appear in the abstract; in everyday terms, these are rules that describe how quantities such as velocity, pressure, heat, or material amount change across space and time. Distributed simulation must solve those rules on neighboring pieces that still agree at their shared borders. The tradeoff is load balance versus communication versus temporal stability. Improving one can hurt another, so the method uses geometric assignment to find partitions that make the conflict manageable.
113.dots: This paper connects to physical simulation because it supports the large calculations behind liquids, flames, and explosions. It connects to geometry because the active domain is a changing shape that must be divided into useful cells. It also connects to systems work in graphics: the visual result depends on how computation is spread across machines, not only on the physical equations themselves. Neighboring SIGGRAPH papers on sampling and acceleration share the same pressure: spend work where it matters, avoid empty space, and keep approximations stable enough for production. The power diagram also relates to other region-division methods, such as image diagrams, because both ask which center owns which part of a continuous domain. The deeper shared idea is constraint balancing: equal work, low boundary exchange, and smooth time behavior must all be true enough at once.
113.ww: The method should work better than fixed spatial chunks because it adapts ownership to the actual active domain. If the fluid or fire occupies only a thin, moving part of space, weighted cells can follow that distribution instead of wasting nodes on empty boxes. Optimal transport gives a principled way to balance amounts, so the partitioner is not just chasing local fixes. Power-diagram cells remain geometric regions, which helps keep communication understandable: neighboring cells share boundaries where data must pass. The temporal consistency goal addresses the common failure of aggressive rebalancing, where partitions become even at one frame but change too sharply by the next. By measuring surface index and temporal consistency index, the paper also makes the quality tradeoff explicit.
